title: Outsourcing and the Globalizing Legal Profession
author: Jayanth K. Krishnan

st.t: Outsourcing fees: Delegation cannot justify double recovery
st.an: The source does not address the cluster’s central billing proposition about service fees, pass-through costs, or double recovery. Instead, it redirects the ethical inquiry toward American outsourcers’ responsibilities to India’s legal system, distinguishing workers’ private gains from broader institutional investment.
qs: As we will see, the ethical obligations discussed here are very different and go to the question of what the American legal outsourcers' responsibility is to the Indian legal environment and system upon which they draw.
The question is how much of this revenue is dedicated to improving the country's legal system-likely very little.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess legal AI’s jagged capabilities, verification needs or human–AI operating-model redesign. Although it describes selective outsourcing of routine legal tasks and resulting professional restructuring, it redirects the inquiry toward globalization and the institutional responsibility of outsourcing beneficiaries to strengthen India’s justice system.
qs: As we will see, the ethical obligations discussed here are very different and go to the question of what the American legal outsourcers' responsibility is to the Indian legal environment and system upon which they draw.

This model argues that though it is important to have good people on staff, the fact that the legal work is not complex, extensive training of Indian employees is required anyway, and the market is filled with competent individu- als who can perform these rather simple tasks, means that hiring decisions should be based on whether the person has common sense and is collegial rather than on whether she is a lawyer.

st.t: Legal outsourcing: Commercial growth need not advance workers
st.an: Krishnan supports the core distinction between outsourcing’s commercial rewards and broader advancement: benefits reach only a limited group, while professional transformation depends conditionally on greater specialisation rather than following automatically from market growth. He is more optimistic than the cluster’s worker-focused studies about possible professional change.
qs: For those who are fortunate to benefit from legal outsourcing,the payoffs are indeed rewarding.But most Indians, of course, are not participants in--or beneficiaries of-this practice.

Presuming that more specialization occurs, which will likely lead to more competition, innovation, and a possible transformation of the Indian legal profession, legal outsourcing then will have had an influencing effect.

kp.k: Legal outsourcing encompasses multiple organizational models and task levels
kp.d: This 2007 article examines human legal outsourcing, not AI. Krishnan identifies three principal arrangements connecting American clients to India: corporate subsidiaries employing Indian legal personnel, direct contracting with Indian lawyers or firms, and third-party intermediaries delivering outsourced services. He argues that outsourcing extends beyond routine administrative work to patent applications, transactional matters and appellate briefs. Domestic outsourcing also exists, including work assigned to American professors and contract lawyers.
qs: This Article shall argue that there are many forms to the legal outsourcing model and a range of legal services that can be provided.

Sometimes referred to as legal processing outsourcing (LPO) companies, these third-party vendors serve as intermediaries between the American corporation or American law firm looking to outsource and Indians eager to do the work.

kp.k: Growth forecasts rest on uncertain employment definitions
kp.d: The article reports 12,000 legal jobs outsourced abroad in 2004 and a research firm's projection approaching 80,000 by 2015. India-specific estimates vary: one report counts around 1,800 workers and projects 24,000 by 2010, while another reports fewer than 12,000 and forecasts 79,000 by 2015. Krishnan cautions that these figures do not consistently distinguish lawyers from administrative personnel or establish India as the destination of all projected jobs. A footnote attributes a projected 40,400 American lawyer job losses by 2015 to Forrester Research's May 2004 study.
qs: In 2004 alone, 12,000 legal jobs were outsourced abroad, and by 2015 one research firm estimates that the total number will near 80,000.
Because these figures are so varied and do not indicate whether those employed are lawyers, it is difficult to know the extent to which American legal outsourcers have penetrated the Indian bar.

kp.k: Cost pressures encourage relocating both support and substantive work
kp.d: Reported examples include GE saving over two million dollars through its Indian in-house legal office, DuPont assigning patent applications and novelty searches to Indian lawyers, and West employing Indian lawyers to summarize unpublished American rulings. An OfficeTiger/Hildebrandt table estimates annual spending of $19.92 billion across eleven support and legal-service categories at the top 200 American firms by gross revenue. Interview-based comparisons place complicated patent applications at $8000–$10,000 in the Midwest, up to $12,000 in Silicon Valley, and $5000–$6000 when outsourced to India. These are contemporary reported estimates, not controlled cost-effectiveness findings.
qs: In 2004, the megalegal publish- ing corporation, West, opened an office in Mumbai (Bombay) where Indian lawyers were hired to prepare synopses of unpublished American court rulings.
One LPO executive, who asked that he and his company remain anonymous, reported that the salaries for his personnel in India range from $2500 per year to only as high as $35,000-$40,000 per year.

kp.k: India's attractiveness extends beyond lower labor costs
kp.d: Krishnan attributes India's position to English-language capabilities, technological infrastructure, political democracy, legal traditions connected to Britain and the United States, and the economic liberalization launched in 1991. He also reports multiple-year tax holidays, import/export duty exemptions, and assurances against bureaucratic obstruction and bribery demands. These institutional advantages underpin his later argument that outsourcing beneficiaries owe obligations to the society supporting their operations.
qs: The low cost of labor, the surge in information technology, favorable macroeconomic policies, the high quality of workers with advanced educations, the democratic system of government, and the historical ties to the United States, are thus all significant factors for why India is fertile ground for American legal outsourcers.

kp.k: Outsourcing creates mixed professional and nonprofessional workforces
kp.d: At Intellevate's New Delhi operation, the article describes about 120 employees: approximately thirty Ph.D.-qualified technical scientists, about twenty lawyers, and several dozen lower-skilled administrative workers. CEO Leon Steinberg says the lawyers previously practiced at reputable firms but now undertake relatively well-paid paralegal roles. Other vendors emphasize elite legal credentials to reassure clients and simplify recruitment. An anonymous entrepreneur instead argues that ordinary competent workers can be trained for simple tasks as readily as elite lawyers, making collegiality and common sense more relevant than legal credentials.
qs: At Intellevate's New Delhi office, for example, there are about 120 employees.
Thirty or so are technical scientists with Ph.D.s who work on intellectual property matters, such as conducting patent novelty searches.
An alternative business model is at play for others who partici- pate in legal outsourcing to India.

kp.k: Client pressure drove a law-firm-founded outsourcing intermediary
kp.d: The empirical case study draws on January 2006 interviews with Intellevate CEO Leon Steinberg and Schwegman partner Steve Lundberg, alongside observation of business operations. Schwegman began experimenting with sending document-preparation tasks to India after identifying their cost burden in 1999, and established the separate Intellevate arrangement in 2003. According to the interviewees, corporate dissatisfaction with patent-prosecution costs prompted the firm to offer outsourcing of low-level work at one-quarter of existing costs to retain clients. Intellevate reportedly served twenty law firms and thirty Fortune 500 corporations.
qs: Second, the firm realized that the practice of patent prosecution was changing and that it needed to be at the forefront of this shift.
To corporate executives, so much of the lawyers' work seemed pedestrian; yet legal costs continued to rise.

kp.k: Dedicated teams coexist with shared administrative services
kp.d: Intellevate allocated work between Minneapolis and New Delhi on a cost-benefit basis. Its eleven-and-one-half-hour time difference reportedly supported turnaround within twenty-four hours. For specialized or confidential work, Indian employees were exclusively assigned to individual American clients; Schwegman had twenty such workers, comprising fifteen paralegals and five technical patent engineers. Simpler administrative requests went to a separate shared-services operation. Tasks included patent and trademark support, docketing, technical research, proofreading and accounting. The article reports CPA's August 2005 controlling-stake acquisition as evidence of the business's commercial development.
qs: In terms of allocating specific work between Minneapolis and New Delhi, decisions are made on a cost-benefit basis.
Clients whose work is delegated to this shared services department tend to have simpler and general administrative needs.

kp.k: Supervision-based ethical views are reported, not comprehensively resolved
kp.d: Krishnan distinguishes his concern with obligations to India's legal environment from conventional professional-responsibility questions such as confidentiality, conflicts, disclosure, supervision, malpractice and discipline, which he attributes to other scholarship. He reports Geoffrey Hazard's view that location may matter little when outsourced workers act under American lawyers' supervision. He also notes that India restricts practice by lawyers licensed only in the United States, explaining why a foreign-resident American contract-lawyer model is less applicable there. These are reported contemporary positions, not a general finding that outsourcing complies with every professional rule.
qs: As we will see, the ethical obligations discussed here are very different and go to the question of what the American legal outsourcers' responsibility is to the Indian legal environment and system upon which they draw.

The argument that both the government and the bar have made is that, because Indian-licensed lawyers are not permitted to practice in the United States, India has no obligation to extend the courtesy to U.S.-only licensed lawyers.

kp.k: Commercial outsourcing gains coexist with unmet domestic justice needs
kp.d: Krishnan argues that outsourcing's rewards reach a small segment of Indians while the wider population faces expensive, delayed justice. The article cites approximately 20,000 pending Supreme Court cases, three million in state High Courts, and twenty-four million in lower courts, two-thirds of the latter criminal. Its 2004 state-level data show severe congestion even in economically successful outsourcing locations. A 2004 Law Commission report is cited for the claim that 70% of jailed people were under-tried prisoners. These historical statistics support the article's distinction between commercial legal-service growth and improvements in public access to justice.
qs: For the vast majority of Indians, legal outsourcing has no relevance in their everyday lives.
In the Supreme Court alone there are about 20,000 cases pending.
These hundreds of millions of Indians need better access to the legal process and less delay in the amount of time their cases are adjudicated.

kp.k: Procedural incentives and inadequate capacity sustain court congestion
kp.d: The article resists explaining backlog simply through excessive litigation, citing comparative and historical work suggesting low Indian civil filing rates. Instead, it emphasizes government litigation and appeals, permissive interlocutory procedures, lawyers paid per court appearance, judicial vacancies and inadequate infrastructure. It reports roughly 13,000 lower district courts facing twenty-four million pending cases, twelve judges per million people and nearly 5000 vacancies in district courts and state High Courts. Proposed explanations for underfunding include both governmental priorities and competing fiscal demands; Krishnan does not settle between them.
qs: Most observers agree that the main issue in India is not how many cases enter the courts, but how few come out.
The tradition of prolonged appeals continues today in independ- ent India.
These lawyers are in part motivated to keep litigation pending because of the way the Indian Bar organizes its fee structure-lawyers typically receive payment per court appear- ance.

kp.k: Disposal statistics do not establish justice reform success
kp.d: Drawing on more than two years of prior fieldwork with Marc Galanter, Krishnan challenges favorable claims about Lok Adalats, or people's courts. He reports inconsistent statistics, inadequate qualitative evaluation, arbitrary and heavy-handed decision-making, and dissatisfied participants. The critique distinguishes increasing case disposal from delivering satisfactory substantive justice. He also calls for rigorous assessment of commercial arbitration and of the 2002 procedural amendments intended to curb interlocutory appeals, rather than assuming these alternatives solve the courts' problems.
qs: In our two-plus years of field work in India, we rarely found government officials concerned with qualitatively evaluating the substantive outcomes of Lok Adalat decisions or with under- standing how the parties themselves view the process.
Instead these officials praised the success and efficiency of Lok Adalats by pointing to the high number of cases disposed of.

kp.k: Corporate responsibility supplies an ethical rationale for contribution
kp.d: Krishnan reviews competing theories rather than presenting an uncontested obligation: Milton Friedman's shareholder-centered position questions corporate social mandates, while stakeholder and social-responsibility approaches consider effects on employees, consumers and surrounding communities. Drawing especially on Lawrence Mitchell, Krishnan argues that outsourcing businesses benefiting from India's labor, education and institutional environment should contribute to legal reform. He acknowledges that outsourcing already creates income and employment and extends the proposed obligation to other foreign investors receiving comparable advantages.
qs: American law firms, companies, and third-party vendors that outsource legal work to India do not do so in a vacuum.
Assuming that other types of foreign investors hold similar advan- tages, however, there is no reason that they ought to be exempt from the obligation to help.

kp.k: Judicial reform also serves investors' economic interests
kp.d: Krishnan argues that weak courts threaten contract enforcement, confidentiality agreements and timely resolution of business disputes. He reports that SpectRx decided against outsourcing to India partly because of enforcement concerns, and discusses lengthy litigation involving Cogentrix and Coca-Cola. Cogentrix's departure in December 1999 is attributed partly to repeated appeals and delay. The article expressly does not resolve the substantive merits of these disputes and acknowledges that corporate lawyers themselves used delaying tactics. These examples motivate an economic argument for reform, not a measured estimate of its investment effects.
qs: The question, however, is after how much time?
Rather, the point of significance is the length of time that parties like Cogentrix and Coke, as well as their opponents, must wait before hearing final judgments on the petitions filed in court.

kp.k: A governance levy could finance targeted legal reform
kp.d: Krishnan proposes, rather than documents an implemented policy, a progressive good governance fee on American businesses benefiting from outsourcing. It should be calibrated not to deter investment and directed toward judicial training, judges and courtrooms, research on procedural delay, or legal aid. An interest-bearing legal-aid fund is suggested by analogy with American IOLTA programs. He acknowledges that higher costs could make outsourcing to India less attractive; an anonymous vendor argues that emphasizing investors' benefits would secure more support than appealing to altruism.
qs: It could impose what might be called a "good governance fee."
The fee would be progressive in nature and would have to be calculated in a way so as not to deter current or future rates of foreign investment.
Another alternative would be to use the fee to provide legal aid to the large portions of the population that lack the necessary resources to ensure their legal rights are safeguarded.

kp.k: Specialization could transform providers and displace intermediaries
kp.d: Krishnan predicts that continued outsourcing may create specialized Indian legal professionals, including nonlawyers, within a profession historically oriented toward individual courtroom practice. An anonymous American vendor offers a more specific conditional forecast: Indian workers who master patent drafting could leave intermediaries, create their own firms, hire a cheaper American-licensed lawyer to sign off on work, and compete directly for clients. The vendor anticipates lower client prices, possible intermediary obsolescence and greater inequality within India. These are forward-looking arguments, not observed outcomes established by the case study.
qs: Presuming that more specialization occurs, which will likely lead to more competition, innovation, and a possible transformation of the Indian legal profession, legal outsourcing then will have had an influencing effect.

For instance, once these Indian legal workers become familiar enough with how to draft patent applications on their own, they will leave the American vendor, form their own firm, hire a cheaper U.S. -licensed lawyer to sign off on work they do, and compete directly for clients.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: This 2007 source concerns international legal outsourcing, not AI. Krishnan argues that outsourcing reduces legal-service costs and predicts that it may increase specialisation, competition and innovation within the Indian legal profession.
pts.d: In its own domain, the article describes three principal arrangements: corporate subsidiaries employing Indian personnel, direct contracting with Indian firms or workers, and third-party legal outsourcing providers. Work extends beyond administrative tasks to patent applications, research and briefs. Krishnan predicts the emergence of specialised legal professionals, including non-lawyers, while making broader professional transformation conditional on increased specialisation. An anonymous interviewed third-party provider separately predicts that Indian workers could establish competing firms, retain a cheaper U.S.-licensed lawyer to sign off on their work, and potentially eliminate the American intermediary. Krishnan also proposes a good-governance fee on outsourcing businesses to fund Indian judicial reform, arguing that better courts would benefit both investors and the public. These are outsourcing claims and proposals, not claims about AI automation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence combines interviews and a provider case study with secondary reporting, industry estimates and judicial statistics; predictions are not established outcomes.
pts.d: Krishnan examines Intellevate and its founding intellectual-property law firm, drawing particularly on January 2006 interviews with chief executive Leon Steinberg and partner Steve Lundberg. The study describes dedicated and shared-service staffing, task allocation between Minneapolis and New Delhi, and reported client adoption. Reported patent-application prices are $8,000–$10,000 in the Midwest, up to $12,000 in Silicon Valley, and $5,000–$6,000 when outsourced to India. These are interview and news-report figures, not a controlled cost comparison. The article reports inconsistent outsourcing employment estimates and explicitly questions their comparability and occupational coverage. The prediction that Indian providers could displace American intermediaries rests on one anonymous vendor's assessment. Judicial backlog data and examples involving SpectRx, Cogentrix and Coca-Cola support the argument that weak courts can affect investors; they do not demonstrate that the proposed fee would achieve reform. No AI performance evidence is offered.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Observed developments concern the period leading to 2007; market projections extend to 2010 and 2015, while professional transformation and intermediary displacement have no fixed deadline.
pts.d: The article traces offshore legal work to 1995 and describes more structured and specialised outsourcing during the five years preceding publication. It reports industry projections of substantial employment and revenue growth through 2010 and 2015, but notes uncertainty over headcounts, whether workers are lawyers, and whether forecasts concern India alone or all offshore destinations. Continued use of India depends on cost advantages, training, suitable work and supportive investment conditions. The anonymous vendor's displacement scenario depends on Indian workers becoming capable of drafting patent applications independently and arranging U.S.-licensed sign-off. Krishnan's fee proposal is conditional on avoiding deterrence of investment and directing revenue toward useful reforms. He acknowledges that higher costs could cause businesses to reconsider India and that investors may respond more readily to financial self-interest than to ethical arguments.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Outsourcing benefits participating clients, providers and Indian workers, but Krishnan stresses that most Indians do not share those benefits and still lack effective access to justice.
pts.d: U.S. corporate legal departments and law firms, especially those handling intellectual property, seek lower costs and additional service capacity. Third-party outsourcing providers gain business but, according to the anonymous interviewee, could eventually face direct competition from Indian specialists. Indian lawyers, paralegals, technical scientists and administrative workers gain employment, income and specialised experience; some trained lawyers perform work below their formal qualification level. The anonymous vendor anticipates that profitable specialist firms could widen economic disparities. Krishnan distinguishes these commercial benefits from the needs of ordinary Indians facing delayed proceedings and inadequate legal infrastructure. His proposed fee would support legal aid, judicial education, additional judges and courtrooms, and research into procedural reform, while potentially improving investors' ability to enforce contracts and resolve disputes.
